article.overview:
A descent camera records what a spacecraft sees as it falls toward the surface, from the point at which the view first contains useful ground detail until touchdown. Its images show the approach terrain, the landing area and effects such as dust lifted by the engine exhaust. Descent imagery is therefore a record of the landing itself, and in some cases it shows where the vehicle came down relative to nearby features [9].

The Apollo lunar missions carried the best-documented lunar descent camera. Each Apollo Lunar Module carried a 16 mm Maurer Data Acquisition Camera (DAC), which was used to record the descent, the ascent and some surface operations [2]. For Apollo 11, the camera was activated 14 minutes 43 seconds before touchdown [2]. On Mars, Malin Space Science Systems (MSSS) built a Mars Descent Imager (MARDI) that has flown on three landers with three different outcomes. On Mars Polar Lander (1999), the lander was lost on arrival [1]. MSSS states that MARDI's descent images could be returned only if the landing succeeded [8], so, by inference, none was returned from that flight. On Phoenix (2008), MARDI was not operated during entry, descent and landing [6][7]. On the Mars Science Laboratory rover Curiosity (2012), MARDI returned color descent images that JPL released in August 2012 [10][11].

Chandrayaan-3's lander sensor suite lists a Lander Horizontal Velocity Camera (LHVC) and a Lander Hazard Detection and Avoidance Camera (LHDAC) [12]. The sources verified for this article give no specifications for either camera, and their descent-imaging roles are not confirmed by a primary ISRO document. The hazard camera is covered in payload 031.
article.description:
A descent camera is a framing camera mounted on a lander, a lander-borne vehicle or a rover, so that it looks down or forward through the approach. In the Apollo case the camera was a film camera mounted inside the Lunar Module. It was set up for the window view, not for a separately deployed platform. On the Mars missions the camera was a solid-state (CCD) imager with its own electronics, operated on a timed sequence through the descent. Each of these instruments records a series of frames over time, and the frame sequence is what relates an image to the stage of the descent at which it was taken [2][5][11].

The Apollo DAC was a 16 mm motion-picture camera with an 18 mm wide-angle lens, a film magazine and automatic frame-rate settings [2]. The MARDI instruments were small digital cameras. The Mars Polar Lander MARDI used a Kodak KAI-1001 CCD of 1024 × 1024 pixels with 9 µm pixels [5]. The Mars Science Laboratory MARDI used a Bayer-pattern CCD array of 1600 × 1200 pixels to produce color images [9].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications:
The primary purpose of a descent camera is to record the approach and the landing. Its images can show the local terrain at a scale that orbital images do not resolve. They can also show the behaviour of the landing system, including dust lifted by the engines [3][11]. MSSS describes the MSL MARDI as intended to show where the rover landed, how far it was from geologic features of interest, and what wind it encountered during descent, and to help plan early traverses [9].

Descent imagery has three main uses. The first is operational: confirming the landing position and the immediate surroundings. The second is scientific: recording the local geology and surface texture in the final minutes. The third is engineering: documenting the performance of the descent system, such as the separation of the heat shield [10]. The sources verified for this article do not describe a generic descent camera specification for any one of these uses, so the purposes above are general descriptions of the class and not measured results.

The Apollo DAC footage also served as a record of the crew's actions during descent and on the surface, because the same camera was used for surface operations [2].
article.operating_principle:
A descent camera converts light from the approach scene into a stored or transmitted image sequence. In the Apollo case, light passed through a lens in the Lunar Module window and exposed 16 mm film. The camera was run at a selected frame rate and shutter speed. For the Apollo 11 descent, the Apollo 11 flight plan set the camera to 6 frames per second with infinity focus [2]. The DAC offered automatic frame rates of 1, 6 and 12 frames per second, and a semi-automatic rate of 24 frames per second, with shutter speeds between 1/60 and 1/1000 second [2].

In the MARDI instruments, light is focused by a lens onto a CCD, and the image is read out and stored or transmitted. The Mars Polar Lander MARDI used a lens with an effective focal length of 7.01 mm and an f/5.6 aperture, and gave a nominal field of view of 65.9 degrees over a 9 mm square photoactive area [5]. The MSL MARDI Bayer filter provides the color data. The MSSS page for that instrument does not state its lens focal length or field of view [9].

Timing is part of the operating principle. The Mars Polar Lander MARDI design specified a frame time of 0.5 seconds for heat-shield jettison, 5.3 seconds during parachute descent and 4.0 seconds during powered descent [5]. These are design values, and no measured timing was reported in the sources read for this article.
article.scientific_importance:
Descent imagery provides context that other instruments cannot. A radar or spectrometer on a lander records properties of the surface beneath it. A descent camera records the shape and texture of the surface as it approaches, and it can link a surface measurement to the wider terrain. This is why descent imaging is valued in planetary exploration, even though the observation lasts only minutes.

The Apollo DAC footage recorded the descents of the Apollo lunar landings, including the dust raised by the descent engine as the Apollo 11 vehicle approached the surface [2][3]. The MSL MARDI images are among the first color images that the rover sent back from Mars after its landing. They show the rocket-exhaust dust cloud and the heat shield as seen during the sky-crane descent [10][11]. The MSSS description of the Phoenix instrument states that it was designed to photograph the northern plains landing site during descent [8]. That imaging did not take place [6][7], so the Phoenix case is a lesson about the spacecraft interface rather than about terrain.

physical_specifications.note:
There is no universal mass, size, power, lens or frame rate for a descent camera. Each example below is a named instrument, and each value is tied to its source. Where a value is not stated in the sources read, the example says so. The examples are not directly comparable, because they fly on different vehicles, use different detector technologies and were built for different descent profiles.

The status of each example is set out in its heading. The Apollo DAC is a flown lunar instrument. The three MARDI examples are flown Mars instruments with different outcomes. The Chandrayaan-3 entry is a flown lander camera with no published specifications in the sources read. No flight-qualified, prototype or proposed lunar descent camera is included, because none was verified with a primary source in this run.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: The Apollo DAC object is 22.9 × 13.7 × 9.7 cm overall, for the Apollo 14 unit [4]. The Mars Polar Lander MARDI is 6 × 8 × 12 cm [5]. The MSL MARDI dimensions are not stated on the MSSS page read [9]. The Phoenix and Chandrayaan-3 dimensions are not publicly specified in the sources read.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: The Apollo DAC with its 130-foot magazine weighed 2.8 pounds, about 1.27 kg [2]. The Mars Polar Lander MARDI mass is 480 g [5]. The MSL MARDI mass is not stated [9]. The Phoenix and Chandrayaan-3 masses are not publicly specified in the sources read.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: The Mars Polar Lander MARDI is listed at 3.5 W while imaging in one table and about 3 W while imaging in an interface section [5]. The Apollo DAC power draw is not publicly specified in the sources read. The MSL, Phoenix and Chandrayaan-3 power values are not publicly specified in the sources read.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen:
Descent cameras operate in the lander's most dynamic phase. The Apollo camera operated in the vacuum of the lunar environment, and the MARDI instruments operated in the thin Martian atmosphere. Both are exposed to the engine exhaust and the dust it lifts. The MSL image of the dust cloud from the sky-crane rocket motors shows that the descent imager sees the plume effects directly [11]. The Apollo 11 source page likewise notes dust being picked up and blown away from the lander's rocket engines [3].

Thermal and power constraints matter for electronic descent cameras. The Mars Polar Lander MARDI specification gives a power figure while imaging [5]. The Phoenix MARDI was not operated, and the source attributes this to "technical concerns on the spacecraft side of the interface" [7]. The thermal environment of the Apollo DAC is not publicly specified in the sources read.

The camera's viewing geometry is an operational requirement. The Apollo DAC looked through a Lunar Module window, so its view was set by that window [2][4]. The MSL MARDI is mounted on the outside of the rover body, so its view depends on the rover's position and orientation during descent [9]. Timing is also an operational requirement. The Mars Polar Lander MARDI specification gives separate frame times for each phase of descent [5].
article.limitations:
A descent camera records a short window of time. The Apollo DAC was limited by its film magazine, which could record about 88 minutes at 1 frame per second [2]. The Apollo 11 descent was 14 minutes 43 seconds long, so the magazine was sufficient for the descent but not for a long surface sequence [2].

The MARDI instruments depend on the lander's descent sequence. The Mars Polar Lander MARDI produced no returned descent imagery because the lander was lost on arrival [1][8]. The Phoenix MARDI was not operated, so its descent view is unavailable [6][7]. A descent image is therefore only as useful as the landing that carries it.

The MSL MARDI images were downsized for transmission, and full-resolution versions were to follow later [10]. The sources do not state the transmission schedule. The Apollo DAC footage is film, and the sources read do not describe a digital copy or processing of the full descent sequence.

Lens and field-of-view values for the Apollo DAC conflict between sources. The MSSS history page gives an 18 mm lens [2]. A search summary of a different Apollo source gave a 10 mm lens for the lunar module camera. That source was not verified in full, so the 18 mm value is the one recorded here, with the conflict listed in the final section.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A descent camera is not a separately deployed surface payload in the Apollo case. The DAC was carried inside the Lunar Module and used through its window [2][4]. The Mars MARDI instruments were mounted on the landers or the rover. For a future lunar descent camera, its transportation would depend on the lander's mounting points, field of view, power and data interfaces, none of which is verified for any named lander in this article.
transportation_process: Integrate the camera into the lander or vehicle on Earth.
Transfer toward the Moon or Mars.
Land, with the camera operating through the final descent.
Transmit or store the descent imagery.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: The Apollo DAC was not deployed separately. It was mounted in the Lunar Module window [2][4]. The MSL MARDI was mounted on the outside of the rover body [9]. The Phoenix MARDI was carried on its lander, and no deployment of the instrument is described in the sources read [6][7]. Mounting for a future descent camera would have to be defined for the specific lander.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Apollo DAC is the main lunar example, with the Apollo 14 unit documented in the Smithsonian collection [4] and the Apollo 11 descent described by MSSS [2][3]. The MARDI instruments provide the Mars examples, with the 2012 MSL images as the best-documented descent imaging [10][11]. The Chandrayaan-3 lander is listed with its cameras [12].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: This article does not assert compatibility between a descent camera and any named lander, rover or spacecraft. The Apollo DAC is recorded as part of the Lunar Module, but the interface details for other landers are not verified. A future descent camera would need its mass, dimensions, mounting points, field of view, power and data interfaces checked against verified lander specifications before any compatibility claim is made.

article.historical_significance:
The Apollo DAC is the best-documented lunar descent camera in the sources read, and it recorded the descents and landings of the Apollo lunar missions [2][3][4]. The Apollo 11 descent imagery is a historical record of the first crewed landing, and the DAC footage captured the crew's approach and touchdown [2][3].

On Mars, the MARDI sequence shows the range of outcomes for a descent camera. The Mars Polar Lander MARDI was flown but its imagery was not returned because the lander was lost on arrival [1][8]. The Phoenix MARDI was flown but was not operated during descent [6][7]. The MSL MARDI returned color descent imagery in 2012, which JPL released [10][11].

The Chandrayaan-3 lander sensors, including the LHVC and LHDAC, form part of a later lunar landing system. Their specific descent-imaging performance is not published in the sources read [12].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties:
- **Apollo DAC specifications.** The DAC data come from one MSSS history page [2] and one Smithsonian object record [4]. The power draw, electrical interface and thermal control are not publicly specified in the sources read.
- **Apollo DAC lens.** The MSSS page gives 18 mm [2]. A search summary of a different Apollo source gave 10 mm for the lunar module camera. That source was not verified in full, so the conflict remains open.
- **Apollo 11 descent montage.** The montage is hosted on an MSSS page and credited to NASA/JSC [3]. The page does not name the frame numbers or the camera, so the link to the DAC is an inference from the page's subject.
- **MPL MARDI status.** The statement that no descent images were returned is inferred from MSSS's note that images could be returned only after a successful landing [8] and from NASA's report that the lander was lost on arrival [1]. The sources read do not state directly that no images were returned.
- **MPL MARDI specifications.** The values in Example 2 are design or heritage values from one MSSS page [5]. The page reports conflicting power figures and a focal-length label conflict. They are not confirmed flight measurements.
- **Phoenix MARDI.** The mass, power, detector, lens, field of view and frame rate are not publicly specified in the sources read. The MSSS instrument description was labelled forthcoming [8]. The project page states that the instrument was not operated during entry, descent and landing [6][7].
- **MSL MARDI specifications.** The mass, power, lens, field of view, frame rate and buffer size are not stated on the MSSS instrument description page [9]. The footprints given there are design or nominal values, not measured results.
- **Chandrayaan-3 cameras.** The LHVC and LHDAC are listed by ISRO without specifications [12]. The descent-imaging role of the LHVC is reported in secondary press coverage only and is not confirmed by a primary ISRO document.
- **No lunar flight-qualified, prototype or proposed descent cameras.** No primary source was verified for a flight-qualified, prototype or proposed lunar descent camera in this run. The article therefore does not present any such design as an example.
- **Images.** Five direct image assets were checked, each with HTTP 200 and a visual match to the source-page description. The two JPL source pages for the MSL images (PIA15988 and PIA15990) returned HTTP 403 to the automated URL check, so their content was read through a page-reading tool rather than confirmed by HTTP 200. The MSSS source pages for the other three images returned HTTP 200. Other images referenced in the research, including an Apollo 11 DAC frame in the NASA image library, could not be verified as direct assets and are not displayed.
- **Full-resolution downloads.** Only the JPEG files linked from the JPL and MSSS pages were checked. Full TIFF downloads were not checked.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url, source_page_url and reference URLs in this file have query strings and fragments removed. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery. Image objects are identical copies of the registry entries.

data_quality_notes: Open gap 1 (Apollo DAC): the DAC data rest on one MSSS history page and one Smithsonian object record. The 18 mm lens (MSSS) conflicts with a 10 mm value in a search summary that was not verified. Power, electrical interface and thermal control are not publicly specified in the sources read. No NASA primary technical report for the DAC was verified; the NASA JSC DAC PDF returned HTTP 404 and the ALSJ DAC page had no DAC content.

Open gap 2 (Mars Polar Lander MARDI): the statement that no descent images were returned is an inference from the MSSS note on return conditions and the NASA loss-on-arrival statement, not a direct statement. The MARDI heritage specifications come from one MSSS page with conflicting power values and a focal-length label conflict; they are design values, not flight measurements.

Open gap 3 (flight-qualified, prototype and proposed classes): no primary source was verified for a flight-qualified, prototype or proposed lunar descent camera in this run. The Chandrayaan-3 LHVC and LHDAC have no published specifications in the ISRO listing page read; the LHVC descent-imaging role rests on secondary press coverage only. The MSL MARDI mass, power, lens, field of view, frame rate and buffer are not stated on the MSSS page read.

Phoenix MARDI: the MSSS pages state it was not operated during entry, descent and landing. The Phoenix instrument description page was labelled forthcoming, so no Phoenix-specific specifications are recorded.

Images: five registry images, each with a direct asset URL that returned HTTP 200 and was visually checked. The two JPL source pages (PIA15988 and PIA15990) returned HTTP 403 to the automated URL check; their content was read through a page-reading tool, so their HTTP status is not confirmed. The other source pages returned HTTP 200 and identify the asset. The Apollo 11 montage is hosted on an MSSS page with NASA/JSC credit; public-domain status is not asserted. The two JPL MARDI JPEGs are served from a CDN host linked by the JPL pages. Full-resolution TIFF downloads were not checked.

Not included as image objects: an Apollo 11 DAC frame (AS11-36-5389) was referenced in search results but could not be verified as a direct asset. Two NASA-hosted candidate URLs for it returned HTML error pages rather than images.
Cross-references: payload 030 (Navigation camera) and payload 031 (Hazard detection camera). The LHDAC is described in payload 031 scope only. No lander-compatibility claim is made for any example.
Validation: the Markdown and JSON were generated from the same text. The validator checks catalogue match, section order, URL cleanliness, image placements and citation coverage.
